title: Eulerian polynomial conjecture for the matrices $N_k$
statement:
For each $k$, let $N_k$ be the matrix appearing in the expression for the generating series $\mathcal{R}_k(t)$, and write $\pi_{N_k}(t)$ and $\chi_{N_k}(t)$ for its minimal and characteristic polynomials. Let $\mathrm{Eul}_{k}(t)$ denote the Eulerian polynomial. **Eulerian $N_k$-matrix conjecture.** The minimal and characteristic polynomials coincide and satisfy

$$
\pi_{N_k}(t)=\chi_{N_k}(t)=(-1)^k t\,\mathrm{Eul}_{k}(-t).
$$

The conjecture is motivated by the explicit initial matrices and their apparent connection with Eulerian polynomials; the source gives no proof or resolution.

progress.summary:
Hivert and Pilaud formulated the conjecture in 2019, asserting that the two polynomials attached to each matrix $N_k$ coincide and equal the stated Eulerian expression. Their source presents the claim as a conjecture, not a proved theorem.

*[arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/1906.02228)*

**Posted attempt**

A reader-written argument claims a complete proof over characteristic-zero fields: it expresses $N_k$ as a rank-one perturbation of the Pascal matrix, derives the characteristic polynomial using the determinant lemma and the Eulerian generating function, then proves equality with the minimal polynomial via a cyclic vector. The argument has not been independently verified.

Current status (as of August 2026): The conjecture has a complete-proof claim, but its correctness remains unverified and no independently corroborated resolution is recorded.

*Caveats. The claimed proof appears only in unverified reader-written discussion.*

solutions.body:
# The characteristic and minimal polynomials of the Pascal-difference matrix

Let $k\ge 1$, and work over a field $K$ of characteristic zero. Set

$$
N=N_k=\left[\binom{k}{j}-\binom{i}{j}\right]_{0\le i,j\le k},
$$

where $\binom{i}{j}=0$ for $j>i$. Define the two Eulerian normalizations by

$$
\begin{aligned}
A_k(t)&=\sum_{\sigma\in S_k}t^{\operatorname{des}(\sigma)},\\
E_k(t)&=tA_k(t).
\end{aligned}
$$

Here $\operatorname{des}(\sigma)$ is the number of indices $i<k$ with $\sigma_i>\sigma_{i+1}$. We prove

$$
\begin{aligned}
\pi_N(t)&=\chi_N(t)\\
&=(-1)^{k+1}t^2A_k(-t)\\
&=(-1)^k tE_k(-t).
\end{aligned}
\tag{1}
$$

This is [Hivert–Pilaud, Conjecture 4.36](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1906.02228v2#page=48). Their arXiv version 2 uses $A_k$ in Definition 2.31, whereas Definition 2.30 of the [author manuscript](https://www.ub.edu/comb/vincentpilaud/documents/publications/HivertPilaud_SignaleticOperads.pdf#page=12) uses the shifted polynomial $E_k$. Thus the two displayed forms in (1) express the same identity. The proof uses the classical Eulerian generating function, Pascal's binomial identity, and the rank-one determinant lemma.

## 1. A rank-one perturbation of the Pascal matrix

Let $P=[\binom{i}{j}]_{0\le i,j\le k}$, let $u$ be the column vector whose entries are all $1$, and let $b$ be the column vector with $b_j=\binom{k}{j}$. Then

$$
N=ub^{\mathsf T}-P.
\tag{2}
$$

For every integer $m\ge0$ and every $0\le i\le k$, the binomial theorem gives

$$
(P^mu)_i=(m+1)^i.
\tag{3}
$$

Indeed, the assertion holds for $m=0$, and multiplication by $P$ replaces $(m+1)^i$ by

$$
\sum_{j=0}^i\binom{i}{j}(m+1)^j=(m+2)^i.
$$

In particular,

$$
\begin{aligned}
b^{\mathsf T}P^mu
&=\sum_{i=0}^k\binom{k}{i}(m+1)^i\\
&=(m+2)^k.
\end{aligned}
\tag{4}
$$

## 2. The characteristic polynomial

All power series in this section are formal, in $K[[z]]$; no convergence assumption is needed. Since $I+zP$ has invertible constant term, its inverse is

$$
(I+zP)^{-1}=\sum_{m\ge0}(-z)^mP^m.
$$

The rank-one determinant lemma and the fact that $P$ is lower triangular with diagonal entries $1$ give

$$
\begin{gathered}
\det(I-zN)=(1+z)^{k+1}\\
{}\cdot\bigl(1-zb^{\mathsf T}(I+zP)^{-1}u\bigr).
\end{gathered}
\tag{5}
$$

The classical Eulerian identity, recalled as Proposition 2.34 in arXiv version 2 of the source, is

$$
\sum_{r\ge1}r^k w^r
=\frac{wA_k(w)}{(1-w)^{k+1}}.
\tag{6}
$$

Removing its $r=1$ term and dividing by $w$ yields

$$
1+w\sum_{m\ge0}(m+2)^k w^m
=\frac{A_k(w)}{(1-w)^{k+1}}.
$$

Use (4) in (5), and then substitute $w=-z$ in this last identity. The factors $(1+z)^{k+1}$ cancel, so

$$
\det(I-zN)=A_k(-z).
\tag{7}
$$

Consequently,

$$
\chi_N(t)=t^{k+1}A_k(-1/t).
$$

Reversing the positions of a permutation replaces its number of descents by $k-1$ minus that number. Hence

$$
A_k(t)=t^{k-1}A_k(1/t).
$$

Applying this reciprocity to the preceding expression for $\chi_N$ gives

$$
\chi_N(t)=(-1)^{k+1}t^2A_k(-t).
\tag{8}
$$

## 3. A cyclic vector gives the minimal polynomial

Put $v_m=P^mu$. By (3), the matrix with columns $v_0,v_1,\ldots,v_k$ has $(i,m)$ entry $(m+1)^i$. It is a Vandermonde matrix, with determinant

$$
\prod_{0\le a<b\le k}(b-a)\ne0.
$$

Thus $v_0,\ldots,v_k$ are linearly independent over $K$. Characteristic zero ensures that all the factors $b-a$ are nonzero.

Equations (2) and (4) give the exact relation

$$
Nv_m=(m+2)^k u-v_{m+1}.
\tag{9}
$$

Starting from $v_0=u$, induction on $m$ using (9) shows that

$$
v_m\in\operatorname{span}_K
\{u,Nu,\ldots,N^m u\}.
$$

For $m=0,\ldots,k$, these inclusions show that $u,Nu,\ldots,N^ku$ span the whole $(k+1)$-dimensional space. They are therefore linearly independent: $u$ is a cyclic vector for $N$.

If a nonzero polynomial of degree at most $k$ annihilated $N$, applying it to $u$ would contradict this independence. The minimal polynomial thus has degree at least $k+1$. By the Cayley–Hamilton theorem it divides the monic characteristic polynomial, which has degree $k+1$. Therefore $\pi_N=\chi_N$, completing (1).

The boundary $k=1$ is included: $A_1(t)=1$ and $N_1$ is nonzero with $N_1^2=0$, so both polynomials are $t^2$.
